title: Nugget — 8wk Syrian hamster: watery diarrhoea and a wet tail
presentation: 8-week-old male Syrian hamster, bought from a pet shop four days ago. Profuse watery diarrhoea since yesterday, matted wet fur around the tail, hunched and reluctant to move.

stages.title: Triage the patient
stages.briefing: Weight 88 g. Hunched, eyes half closed, coat matted with liquid faeces from the perineum to the tail base. Skin tent prolonged, mucous membranes tacky. Temperature 36.4°C (low). Abdomen doughy and painful. Recently transported, rehomed and separated from littermates.
stages.prompt: Which findings make this an emergency rather than a husbandry problem?

options.label: Prolonged skin tent with tacky membranes
options.detail: Clinically significant dehydration

options.label: Temperature 36.4°C
options.detail: Hypothermia in a collapsing small mammal

options.label: Profuse watery diarrhoea in an eight-week-old
options.detail: The age and volume that kill hamsters

options.label: Recent transport and rehoming
options.detail: The stressor behind the disease, not the emergency

options.label: Matted perineal fur
options.detail: The sign that names the syndrome, but not what threatens life

stages.explanation: Wet tail kills by dehydration and hypothermia, not by the diarrhoea itself, so the findings that matter first are the skin tent and the temperature. The husbandry history explains why an eight-week-old hamster is ill four days after leaving the shop — stress and a diet change — and it belongs in the plan, but stabilisation comes before aetiology.

stages.title: Choose the tests
stages.briefing: Fluids are running subcutaneously and the hamster is on a heat source.
stages.prompt: Which tests are worth doing in a patient this size?

options.label: Faecal wet mount and direct smear
options.detail: Protozoa, motile spirochaetes, cell debris

options.label: Faecal Gram stain
options.detail: Shifts in flora, spore-forming organisms

options.label: Faecal culture including Lawsonia and Salmonella work-up
options.detail: Names the agent and flags a zoonosis

options.label: Blood glucose from a single drop
options.detail: Hypoglycaemia in a small anorexic patient

options.label: Faecal PCR panel for Lawsonia intracellularis
options.detail: The organism behind proliferative ileitis

options.label: Full biochemistry panel
options.detail: The sample volume is not justifiable in an 88 g dehydrated hamster

options.label: Abdominal radiographs before stabilisation
options.detail: Restraint now costs more than the image is worth

stages.explanation: Sample volume is a clinical decision in an 88 g patient: faeces and one drop of blood answer the useful questions, and a full biochemistry panel would take a volume you cannot spare. The Salmonella question is asked for the household as much as the hamster — a child-facing zoonosis changes the advice you give at the door.

stages.title: Interpret the results
stages.briefing: Faecal wet mount: no protozoa, no motile organisms. Gram stain: mixed flora with an excess of Gram-negative rods. Culture: no Salmonella isolated; heavy Escherichia coli growth. Lawsonia intracellularis PCR positive. Blood glucose 3.1 mmol/L (low). Post-mortem of a littermate that died at the shop: thickened, corrugated ileum.
stages.prompt: Which conclusions do the results support?

options.label: Proliferative ileitis — Lawsonia intracellularis
options.detail: PCR positive with the classic ileal lesion in a littermate

options.label: Stress of transport and rehoming precipitated it
options.detail: The recognised trigger in weanling hamsters

options.label: Hypoglycaemia needs correcting alongside fluids
options.detail: Glucose 3.1 mmol/L in an anorexic weanling

options.label: Salmonellosis is the diagnosis and the household is at risk
options.detail: No Salmonella isolated

options.label: Giardiasis explains the diarrhoea
options.detail: No protozoa on wet mount

stages.explanation: Lawsonia with a corrugated ileum in a littermate is as close to confirmation as this species allows, and the E. coli overgrowth is a passenger on a damaged gut rather than the primary agent. Ruling Salmonella out is worth as much as ruling Lawsonia in, because it settles what you tell a family with young children. The low glucose is the finding that changes the next hour.

stages.title: Commit to a diagnosis
stages.briefing: Lawsonia PCR positive, no Salmonella, heavy E. coli, hypoglycaemia, dehydration and hypothermia in a recently rehomed weanling.

options.label: Proliferative ileitis (wet tail) from Lawsonia intracellularis, stress-precipitated
options.detail: Agent, lesion and trigger together

options.label: Salmonellosis
options.detail: Excluded by culture

options.label: Primary E. coli enteritis
options.detail: Overgrowth on an already damaged ileum, not the primary cause

options.label: Antibiotic-associated dysbiosis
options.detail: This hamster has had no antibiotics

options.label: Dietary diarrhoea from a sudden food change
options.detail: A contributor at most; it does not produce a corrugated ileum

stages.explanation: The diagnosis carries the treatment: fluids, warmth, glucose and nutritional support are what save this hamster, with an antibiotic the ileum will tolerate. Naming the stress trigger is what stops the same thing happening to the next weanling the owner buys, and confirming the absence of Salmonella is what lets the family relax.
